title: Improve unit test speed
body:
This blog post provides a good background / introduction: https://threedots.tech/post/go-test-parallelism/

When I ran the following command
```shell
GOMAXPROCS=1 go test -parallel 128 -p 16 -json ./... | go run github.com/roblaszczak/vgt@latest
```

I got the following output:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3699d855-b791-4c54-a8ed-1057f080773c)

It shows some tests running for a very long time (the darker blue colors), but even of some of them were sped up there are others (like in the first group in top left corner) that are still relatively long.

We also almost never use `t.Parallel()` in our test (right now I only found one instance), even though many of our tests are starting servers and making network calls, so could benefit from parallelism. But adding `t.Parallel()` should be done with care - some tests are starting servers on the same port (instead of ephemeral port) and must be refactored before adding parallelism.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Hello @reporter ,
Some observations:
Usage of t.Parallel(): I've noticed that adding t.Parallel() generally only makes sense in tests with blocking operations, and even then, the impact on overall test speed can be minimal for some cases.
Impact on Test Tables: The most significant improvement in test speed has been within test tables. 
I was able to reduce the test time for the crossdock/services package from 2.859 seconds to 2.760 seconds.
Given these results, I’d like to know if you’d like me to continue refining this package or focus on specific areas. Additionally, do we have a target or expected test time reduction for each package? Knowing this will help me prioritize and make the best use of parallelism where it counts.

comments.author: participant6
comments.body: Hi @reporter , I made my first small PR to improve the tests slightly. Would you mind taking a look? On another note, I notice that the `elasticsearch.TestNewFactory()` takes ~5s every time due to ElasticSearch Client's default timeout during healthcheck. Since it's for testing purposes, do you think it's fair to reduce the timeout to 1s or disable the healthcheck entirely? This could reduce the total test time significantly but since I'm still new, I might be overlooking something. Please advice.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: @participant6 if a test is expecting a real connection to a mock http server then 5s timeout is fine because connection should happen sooner and 5s is just a precaution against busy test runner freezing. But if the test is for "errors" where the connection is not expected to succeed then it's worth fixing. However usually in those tests the failure happens before the HTTP connection is actually made. If a connection is indeed attempted to say non-existing domain name then the test itself is arguably wrong, it should not be doing that - we should simulate initialization error in a different way, e.g. by using a mock client.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
Hi @reporter — I was looking at the test speed improvements and noticed PR #8127 and #8102 already address the `tracegen/worker_test.go` pause reduction.

I ran a quick audit for other patterns that commonly cause slow unit tests in Go:
1. **Tests using `time.Sleep`** with hardcoded durations > 1ms
2. **Tests not calling `t.Parallel()`** where they safely could
3. **Tests with large `time.Duration` constants** in table-driven test cases

Looking at the issue screenshot, the biggest remaining dark blocks seem to be in the top-left cluster. Are those specific packages already being investigated by someone, or is there still room to dig in and identify the next bottleneck? I'd be happy to profile the test suite and propose the next concrete fix if the area is still open.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
Following up on my earlier audit — I ran the test suite and identified a few packages where `t.Parallel()` can be safely added without port conflicts or shared state issues:

- `cmd/anonymizer/app/writer` — tests create temp files, fully isolated
- `cmd/anonymizer/app/uiconv` — same pattern, temp files only  
- `internal/healthcheck` — no network bindings, pure logic tests

Would it be okay to start with these three packages in a single PR? I'll verify each test doesn't share global state or hardcoded ports before adding `t.Parallel()`.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: It's ok to call but we should only do it for tests that really require parallel execution, if the test is already fast there's no reason to run it in parallel, the overhead might actually make it slower.
